claim: Mice use their whiskers to track walls, staying near the center of a winding corridor without training.
source: When the mice are in the center of the corridor, their whiskers can just touch the walls. Mice use their whiskers to track the walls, staying near the center of the winding corridor without training (Sofroniew et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sofroniew et al., 2014

claim: Bilateral photoinhibition of barrel cortex impaired turning performance in response to bends in the corridor.
source: Silencing barrel cortex bilaterally impaired turning in response to bends in the corridor (angle error 8.09 ± 2.22° vs. 3.68 ± 0.55°, p = 6.4*10−4 t-test) (Figure 1d,e).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased angle error during photoinhibition and reference to Figure 1d,e

claim: Performance during barrel cortex photoinhibition was similar to performance after trimming all whiskers.
source: Performance during photoinhibition was similar to performance after trimming all whiskers (angle error 8.09 ± 2.22° vs. 8.83 ± 2.24°, p = 0.52 t-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing angle errors with no significant difference

claim: Bilateral photoinhibition of visual cortex had no effect on turning performance.
source: In contrast, there was no effect on turning performance in response to bilateral photoinhibition of the visual cortex (angle error 3.20 ± 0.79° vs. 3.68 ± 0.55°, p = 0.19 t-test), controlling for non-specific effects of photoinhibition.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no significant difference in angle error

claim: Mice use neural activity in barrel cortex to guide locomotion along the wall.
source: We conclude that mice use neural activity in barrel cortex to guide locomotion along the wall.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from photoinhibition experiments showing impaired performance

claim: Photoactivation of layer 4 barrel cortex evoked up to 8 additional spikes per neuron per second at maximum experienced power.
source: Stimuli consisted of 2-ms laser pulses (10 Hz); at maximum experienced power the photostimulus evoked up to 8 additional spikes per neuron per second in layer 4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by cell-attached recordings during photoactivation

claim: Mice responded to photoactivation of layer 4 by making left and right turns at bends in the illusory corridor.
source: Mice responded to photoactivation of layer 4 by making left and right turns at bends in the illusory corridor (Figure 2b), with slightly lower angle error than when responding to real walls (angle error 2.30 ± 0.85° vs. 3.19 ± 0.55°, p = 0.026 t-test).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing angle errors in illusory vs. real corridors

claim: Running speeds in the illusory corridor were slower than running speeds in the corridor with walls.
source: Running speeds in the illusory corridor were slower (13.2 ± 3.6 cm/s) than running speeds in the corridor with walls (20.4 ± 3.8 cm/s).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of running speed

claim: Photoactivation of parietal or visual cortices did not enable mice to follow bends in the corridor.
source: When parietal (n=3 mice) or visual cortices (n=5 mice) were activated mice did not follow the bends in the corridor (angle error 14.01 ± 1.73° vs. 3.19 ± 0.55°, p = 1.7*10-8 t-test) (Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing significantly higher angle error

claim: The response to photoactivation was not learnt as all mice performed the task from the very first trial.
source: This response to photoactivation was not learnt as all mice performed the task from the very first trial, similarly to how they perform the task with the real walls (Sofroniew et al., 2014), and the reward was provided in each trial independent of behavioral performance.
evidence: Supported by behavioral observation and citation

claim: Unilateral activation of layer 4 with constant power biased running trajectories towards the side of activation.
source: Running trajectories were biased towards the side of the activation, as if the mice were avoiding a wall they were touching on the contralateral side (7.7 mm ± 4.5 mm at 2.0 mW) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of trajectory bias

claim: Activation of parietal or visual cortex did not show an effect on distance from the wall.
source: Activation of the parietal (n=3) or visual cortex (n=5) did not show an effect on distance from the wall (0.7 mm ± 3.8 mm at 2.0 mW) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements showing minimal trajectory bias

claim: Activity in the barrel cortex can guide locomotion.
source: Together, these results show that activity in the barrel cortex can guide locomotion, and suggest that wall distance may be encoded by spike rates in barrel cortex.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from photoactivation experiments

claim: Wall distance may be encoded by spike rates in barrel cortex.
source: Together, these results show that activity in the barrel cortex can guide locomotion, and suggest that wall distance may be encoded by spike rates in barrel cortex.
evidence: Speculative inference from photoactivation experiments

claim: 28% of layer 2/3 ROIs showed significant tuning to wall distance.
source: Overall 564/2019 (28%) of ROIs showed significant tuning to wall distance (p<0.05, ANOVA across trials) (Figure 3d).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data and statistical analysis

claim: 17% of layer 2/3 ROIs were active but not tuned to wall distance.
source: A further 334/2019 (17%) of ROIs were active (90th percentile F/F > 1.0) but were not tuned to wall distance, and the remaining 1121/2019 (55%) ROIs were inactive.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data

claim: 55% of layer 2/3 ROIs were inactive.
source: A further 334/2019 (17%) of ROIs were active (90th percentile F/F > 1.0) but were not tuned to wall distance, and the remaining 1121/2019 (55%) ROIs were inactive.
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data

claim: The peak wall distance preferred by tuned ROIs tiled the length of the whiskers, with a bias towards small distances.
source: The peak wall distance preferred by the tuned ROIs tiled the length of the whiskers, although there was a bias towards small distances (Figure 3f,g).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing distribution of tuning curve peaks

claim: 86% of recorded units showed significant tuning to wall distance during open-loop movements.
source: Of these units, 179 (86%) showed significant tuning to wall distance during open-loop movements of the wall (p<0.05 ANOVA).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and statistical analysis

claim: The majority of units showed activation (72% with modulation > 0.5).
source: The majority of units showed activation (106/148; 72% modulation > 0.5), but a sizable fraction showed suppression or mixed responses (42/148; 28% modulation <0.5).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and modulation index analysis

claim: 28% of units showed suppression or mixed responses (modulation <0.5).
source: The majority of units showed activation (106/148; 72% modulation > 0.5), but a sizable fraction showed suppression or mixed responses (42/148; 28% modulation <0.5).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and modulation index analysis

claim: Units with negative and near-zero modulation indices tended to be found in infragranular layers.
source: Units with negative and near-zero modulation indices tended to be found in infragranular layers (Figure 4i).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data showing laminar distribution

claim: Units showed similar tuning curves under both open-loop and closed-loop conditions.
source: Units showed similar tuning curves under both open-loop and closed-loop (Figure 4—figure supplement 3a,b), with similar average rates over the same wall distances range (107/114; 94% -0.5 < open vs. closed modulation < 0.5) (Figure 4—figure supplement 3c,d).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data comparing open-loop and closed-loop conditions

claim: 31% of all units were significantly modulated by running speed in the absence of walls.
source: A substantial fraction of all units (31%; 46/148) were significantly modulated by running speed in the absence of the walls (Figure 4—figure supplement 4a,b) (Keller et al., 2012; Saleem et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data and citations

claim: Wall distance tuning curves computed during slow running and fast running were similar on average.
source: However, the wall distance tuning curves computed during slow running and fast running were similar on average (modulation index was −0.10 ± 0.55) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4c,d,e).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data comparing tuning curves at different speeds

claim: Spike rate changes in response to interactions with the contralateral wall were consistently greater than to the ipsilateral wall.
source: Spike rate changes in response to interactions with the contralateral wall were consistently greater than to the ipsilateral wall (27/29; 93% contra vs ipsi modulation > 0) (Figure 4—figure supplement 5e,f).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data comparing contralateral and ipsilateral responses

claim: The hemisphere contralateral to the wall is predominantly involved in wall-tracking.
source: This finding is consistent with the results of the unilateral activation experiment, which suggest the hemisphere contralateral to the wall is predominantly involved in wall-tracking.
evidence: Inference drawn from laterality data and unilateral activation experiments

claim: 55% of neurons were strongly modulated by wall direction (absolute direction modulation > 0.2).
source: Some neurons were strongly modulated (82/148, 55% absolute direction modulation > 0.2).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiology data analyzing direction modulation

claim: Barrel cortex encodes both wall position and direction of wall motion.
source: Barrel cortex thus encodes both wall position and direction of wall motion.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from electrophysiology data showing position and direction tuning

claim: Rodents move their whiskers to localize and identify nearby objects.
source: Rodents move their whiskers to localize (Knutsen et al., 2006; O'Connor et al., 2010) and identify (Anjum et al., 2006) nearby objects, and to guide their locomotion along walls and through narrow tunnels (Vincent, 1912; Sofroniew and Svoboda, 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Whiskers are elastic rods with a gradually decreasing thickness as a function of distance from the face.
source: Whiskers are elastic rods with a gradually decreasing thickness as a function of distance from the face (Birdwell et al., 2007; Hires et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: More proximal deflections cause larger forces at the base of the whisker than distal deflections.
source: Because of the whisker taper, more proximal deflections cause larger forces at the base of the whisker than distal deflections (Birdwell et al., 2007; Pammer et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research on whisker mechanics

claim: Objects that are closer to the face trigger higher spike rates in primary sensory neurons.
source: Objects that are closer to the face therefore trigger higher spike rates in primary sensory neurons (Szwed et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Layer 4 is the main thalamocortical recipient layer and contains spatial clusters of neurons termed 'barrels'.
source: Layer (L) 4 is the main thalamocortical recipient layer and contains spatial clusters of neurons, termed 'barrels'.
evidence: Established anatomical knowledge about barrel cortex

claim: There is a one-to-one correspondence between L4 barrels and specific individual whiskers on the face.
source: There is a one-to-one correspondence between L4 barrels and specific individual whiskers on the face (Van der Loos and Woolsey, 1973).
evidence: Supported by citation to foundational research

claim: Passive whisker deflection causes brief, short latency (~10 ms) excitatory responses in neurons across layers of the corresponding barrel column.
source: Passive whisker deflection causes brief, short latency (~10 ms) excitatory responses in neurons across layers of the corresponding barrel column (Simons, 1978; Armstrong-James et al., 1992; De Kock et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior electrophysiology research

claim: Neural responses increase monotonically with the strength of a whisker stimulus.
source: Individual neurons are sensitive to the direction (Simons and Carvell, 1989), amplitude and velocity of whisker deflection, and neural responses increase monotonically with the strength of a whisker stimulus (Simons, 1978).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Deflection of neighboring whiskers causes longer-latency, weaker, excitatory responses and surround suppression.
source: Deflection of neighboring whiskers causes longer-latency, weaker, excitatory responses (Armstrong-James et al., 1992) and surround suppression (Simons, 1985; Moore and Nelson, 1998), implying that neighboring barrel columns can inhibit each other.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: During exploration, mice move their whiskers rhythmically over objects at ~16 Hz.
source: During exploration, mice move their whiskers rhythmically over objects at ~16 Hz (Mitchinson et al., 2011; Sofroniew et al., 2014; Sofroniew and Svoboda, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior behavioral research

claim: Neurons in layer 4 and layer 2/3 of the barrel cortex show activity highly correlated with touch onset during whisker-based pole localization.
source: In a whisker-based pole localization task in head-fixed mice, neurons in layer 4 and layer 2/3 of the barrel cortex show activity highly correlated with touch onset (O'Connor et al., 2010; Crochet et al., 2011; Hires et al., 2015), with larger forces producing more vigorous responses (O'Connor et al., 2013; Peron et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Barrel cortex activity could drive whisker-guided locomotion through the superior colliculus and rubrospinal circuits.
source: Barrel cortex activity could drive whisker-guided locomotion through the superior colliculus and rubrospinal circuits.
evidence: Speculative hypothesis about neural pathways

claim: The tracking accuracy in the illusory corridor was on par or better compared to the real corridor.
source: The tracking accuracy in the illusory corridor was on par or better compared to the real corridor; this may be because the photostimulus provided a stronger distance-dependent signal compared to touch-evoked activity.
evidence: Observation from experimental data with speculative explanation

claim: Downstream layers and brain areas can interpret increases of layer 4 spike rate as increased proximity to a wall on the contralateral side and drive the appropriate turning responses.
source: These experiments show that downstream layers and brain areas can interpret increases of layer 4 spike rate as increased proximity to a wall on the contralateral side and drive the appropriate turning responses.
evidence: Inference drawn from photoactivation experiments

claim: Encoding wall distance with a population of non-monotonic tuning curves that tile the most frequently encountered distances can achieve higher overall encoding accuracy given a fixed metabolic cost.
source: Encoding wall distance with a population of tuning curves that increase monotonically with decreasing wall distance (i.e. sigmoids) would lead to very large metabolic costs when representing small distances. Given a fixed metabolic cost, a population of non-monotonic (i.e. Gaussian) tuning curves that tile the most frequently encountered distances can achieve higher overall encoding accuracy (Ganguli and Simoncelli, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical work

claim: Calcium imaging revealed 28% of neurons as tuned to wall distance, compared to 17% of neurons responding to touch during a pole location discrimination task.
source: Calcium imaging revealed 28% of neurons as tuned to wall distance. Using similar methods, 17% of neurons responded to touch during a pole location discrimination task performed with a single whisker (Peron et al., 2015).
evidence: Comparison of current data with cited prior research

claim: The differences in tuned neuron percentages could arise from the multi-whisker nature of the wall-tracking experiments, the greater complexity of the interactions, or the fact that mice were running during wall-tracking.
source: These differences could arise from the multi-whisker nature of the wall-tracking experiments, the greater complexity of the interactions between the whiskers and the wall compared to the pole, or the fact that mice were running during wall-tracking.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed differences

claim: Wall direction selective neurons could be useful for helping mice determine wall velocity and acceleration.
source: Wall direction selective neurons could be useful for helping the mice determine wall velocity, and acceleration.
evidence: Speculative functional interpretation

claim: Coding for wall distance, velocity, and acceleration could help mice better track walls through control laws that include derivative feedback alongside proportional feedback.
source: Coding for these variables, in addition to wall distance, could help the mice better track the walls through control laws that include derivative feedback alongside proportional feedback (Sofroniew et al., 2014).
evidence: Speculative functional interpretation with citation

claim: The similarity of tuning curves under open-loop and closed-loop conditions suggests that the details of whisker motion are unlikely to be a critical factor.
source: The similarity of tuning curves under open-loop and closed-loop conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), where running direction are different, suggests that the details of whisker motion are unlikely to be a critical factor.
evidence: Inference drawn from comparison of tuning curves under different conditions

claim: Cross-columnar inhibition mediated by multi-whisker interactions could contribute to complex, non-monotonic tuning curves.
source: Another mechanism is based on cross-columnar inhibition mediated by multi-whisker interactions (Simons, 1985; Brumberg et al., 1996; Moore and Nelson, 1998).
evidence: Speculative mechanism with citations to prior research

claim: Individual whiskers have different lengths and touch the wall at different times as it approaches.
source: Individual whiskers have different lengths (Ibrahim and Wright, 1975) and touch the wall at different times as it approaches.
evidence: Supported by citation and logical inference

claim: Neurons driven by long whiskers may be suppressed by neurons driven by shorter whiskers at smaller wall distances, resulting in non-monotonic distance tuning curves.
source: Neurons driven by the long whiskers may be suppressed by neurons driven by the shorter whiskers at smaller wall distances, resulting in non-monotonic distance tuning curves.
evidence: Speculative mechanistic explanation

claim: Cross-laminar excitation and inhibition could contribute to complex tuning curves through interlaminar connections.
source: A third mechanism relies on cross-laminar excitation and inhibition. Neurons in different layers are coupled through interlaminar connections which excite both excitatory neurons and inhibitory interneurons in the target layers (Lefort et al., 2009; Hooks et al., 2011; Feldmeyer et al., 2013; Pluta et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative mechanism with citations to prior research

claim: Over short time scales, synchronous excitation of L4 neurons is expected to drive spikes in L5 neurons.
source: For example, over short time scales the synchronous excitation of L4 neurons (O'Connor et al., 2013; Hires et al., 2015) is expected to drive spikes in L5 neurons (O'Connor et al., 2013).
evidence: Inference based on cited prior research

claim: Over longer time scales, L4 activation promotes mostly inhibition in L5.
source: Over longer time scales L4 activation promotes mostly inhibition in L5 (Pluta et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Cross-columnar and cross-laminar inhibition combined with short-term synaptic plasticity likely help generate the complex representation of distance in the barrel cortex.
source: Cross-columnar and cross-laminar inhibition combined with short-term synaptic plasticity, likely help generate the complex representation of distance in the barrel cortex, which in turn supports wall-tracking behavior.
evidence: Speculative mechanistic explanation

claim: The complex representation of distance in barrel cortex supports wall-tracking behavior.
source: Cross-columnar and cross-laminar inhibition combined with short-term synaptic plasticity, likely help generate the complex representation of distance in the barrel cortex, which in turn supports wall-tracking behavior.
evidence: Inference connecting neural representation to behavior

claim: Neurons were tuned to the distance between the animal snout and the contralateral wall, with monotonic, unimodal, and multimodal tuning curves.
source: Neurons were tuned to the distance between the animal snout and the contralateral wall, with monotonic, unimodal, and multimodal tuning curves.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings from imaging and electrophysiology

claim: This rich representation of object location in the barrel cortex could not be predicted based on simple stimulus-response relationships involving individual whiskers.
source: This rich representation of object location in the barrel cortex could not be predicted based on simple stimulus-response relationships involving individual whiskers and likely emerges within cortical circuits.
evidence: Inference from the complexity of observed tuning curves

claim: The rich representation of object location likely emerges within cortical circuits.
source: This rich representation of object location in the barrel cortex could not be predicted based on simple stimulus-response relationships involving individual whiskers and likely emerges within cortical circuits.
evidence: Inference from the complexity of observed tuning curves

claim: Optogenetic manipulations revealed that barrel cortex plays a role in wall-tracking.
source: Optogenetic manipulations revealed that barrel cortex plays a role in wall-tracking.
evidence: Summary of photoinhibition experimental results

claim: Closed-loop optogenetic control of layer 4 neurons can substitute for whisker-object contact to guide behavior resembling wall tracking.
source: Closed-loop optogenetic control of layer 4 neurons can substitute for whisker-object contact to guide behavior resembling wall tracking.
evidence: Summary of photoactivation experimental results

claim: Mice were housed individually in cages with bedding and running wheels in a reverse light-cycle room.
source: Mice were housed individually in cages with bedding and running wheels (Bio-Serv, Flemington, NJ: K3327 and K3251) in a reverse light-cycle room.
evidence: Description of experimental methods

claim: Mice were restricted to consume 1.0-1.5 ml of water per day.
source: Mice were restricted to consume 1.0-1.5 ml of water per day (Guo et al., 2014), which could either be obtained during behavioral sessions or in supplements after behavioral sessions.
evidence: Description of experimental methods with citation

claim: GCaMP6s has a rise time of 200 ms and a decay time of 600 ms.
source: GCaMP6s has a rise time of 200 ms and a decay time of 600 ms, which means the fast dynamics of neurons will be hard to capture during a calcium imaging experiment (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research on GCaMP6s properties

claim: A single spike yields a ΔF/F of 0.3, with a half decay time of ~600 ms for GCaMP6s.
source: Under similar conditions a single yields a ΔF/F of 0.3, with a half decay time of ~600 ms (Chen et al., 2013), suggesting that a 1.0 ΔF/F threshold corresponds to a train of 3–4 spikes.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: A 1.0 ΔF/F threshold corresponds to a train of 3–4 spikes.
source: Under similar conditions a single yields a ΔF/F of 0.3, with a half decay time of ~600 ms (Chen et al., 2013), suggesting that a 1.0 ΔF/F threshold corresponds to a train of 3–4 spikes.
evidence: Inference based on cited GCaMP6s properties

claim: Recordings spanned layer 2 to layer 5, although the majority of units were located in infragranular layers.
source: Recordings spanned layer 2 to layer 5, although the majority of units were located in infragranular layers (Figure 4—figure supplement 2a).
evidence: Description of electrophysiology recording locations

claim: Baseline and peak spike rates were higher in deeper layer neurons.
source: Baseline and peak spike rates were higher in deeper layer neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2b,c).
evidence: Observation from electrophysiology data

claim: Both false alarm rate of the inter-spike-interval distribution < 1.5% and waveform SNR > 6 were used as quality control metrics.
source: Spike sorting was performed manually, and both false alarm rate of the inter-spike-interval distribution < 1.5% and waveform SNR > 6 were used as quality control metrics (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c,f).
evidence: Description of data analysis methods

claim: With quality control parameters, 95% of the sorted units had a maximum spike rate > 1 Hz.
source: With these parameters 95% of the sorted units had a maximum spike rate > 1 Hz (Figure 4—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Result of applying quality control metrics

claim: Analysis was restricted to periods of running (speed > 3 cm/s), ensuring the mice were actively whisking.
source: As with the imaging experiments, analysis was restricted to periods of running (speed > 3 cm/s), ensuring the mice were actively whisking (Sofroniew et al., 2014).
evidence: Description of data analysis methods with citation
